docs.title: 0001 — Cancel sibling agents when a DAG level fails
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-29 · Status: accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Agents at the same DAG level run through asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True), which waits for every coroutine even after one has raised. When any agent in a level fails, Pipeline.run() discards the whole level's results and propagates the error — so the siblings that kept running produced output that is thrown away, having spent real tokens and real wall-clock time to make it.

This is worse here than in a generic task runner. The library's stated wedge is that every run tells you what it cost; spending money on discarded output is the specific failure the pitch says it prevents. A five-agent level where one agent fails immediately could bill for four full completions.

The complication is PauseExecution. Human-in-the-loop approval is implemented as an exception, and the pause path deliberately collects and persists the results of every sibling in the level so the run can resume from them. Treating it as a failure would cancel exactly the work the resume depends on.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A level cancels its outstanding agents as soon as one finishes with a real error. PauseExecution is not a real error: it is control flow, and a level containing a pause runs to completion as before.

Cancelled siblings are reported positionally as asyncio.CancelledError, and the error-selection pass skips them, so the exception that surfaces always names the agent that actually failed rather than whichever cancellation happened to sort first.

An outer cancellation — a stream() consumer abandoning the generator — also cancels the level's in-flight tasks rather than leaving them running.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Easier: a failing run stops costing money at the point of failure. Abandoning a stream no longer leaks agents. The error a user sees is the causal one.

Harder: an agent's side effects may now be interrupted part-way. Agents that write to external systems must already tolerate this — a timeout or a process death could always cut them off — but the window is now wider in practice. This is documented rather than mitigated: making agent side effects transactional is the agent author's problem, not the orchestrator's.

Also harder: a caller who wanted a sibling's result despite the level failing can no longer get it. Nothing exposed it before either (the results were discarded), so no API regresses, but the option is now foreclosed.

Exit path: the cancellation is one function, _gather_level. Restoring the old behaviour is deleting it and calling asyncio.gather again. If a real use case appears for "let siblings finish", it becomes a Pipeline(fail_fast=False) flag rather than a rewrite.

docs.title: 0002 — Structured output by prompt injection and repair, not provider JSON modes
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-29 · Status: accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
output_schema validated an agent's reply against a Pydantic model and did nothing else. The model was never told what shape to produce — the README's own example worked around this by embedding Model.model_json_schema() into the user prompt by hand — and a single malformed reply raised AgentOutputValidationError, killing the run.

Three ways to close that gap:

  1. Send the schema to the provider as a native response_format / json_schema parameter, which constrains decoding server-side.
  2. Put the schema in the prompt and validate what comes back.
  3. Both, with a runtime capability check per provider.

agentflow's compatibility claim is "any OpenAI-compatible endpoint" — OpenAI, Groq, Together, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM. Native structured-output support across that set is uneven: differently named, differently shaped, differently strict, and absent entirely on older self-hosted stacks. Option 1 would make the headline claim conditional and fail at runtime on endpoints the README tells people to use. Option 3 means maintaining a capability matrix of other people's servers, which is exactly the ecosystem-sized commitment this library exists to avoid.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Option 2. The JSON Schema is appended to the system prompt — last, so the format contract is the final thing the model reads — and the reply is validated locally. On a validation failure, the model is shown its own output and the validation errors and asked to correct itself, bounded by output_retries (default 1).

A reply wrapped in a markdown code fence is unwrapped locally instead of spending a repair round-trip on a formatting artefact. Nothing further is guessed at: digging a JSON object out of surrounding prose is how you silently validate the wrong thing.

Callers who do want a provider's native JSON mode pass it themselves through LLM.generate(**extra), which forwards any keyword straight to the provider. agentflow never sets it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Easier: output_schema works the same way on every OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including local ones. Transient formatting failures stop killing runs. Users no longer hand-write schemas into prompts.

Harder: schema instructions consume prompt tokens on every call, and a repair is a second billed call. Both are counted into the agent's usage and the pipeline budget rather than hidden, but they are real cost. Prompt-level constraint is also weaker than constrained decoding — a determined model can still return prose, which is what the repair round is for.

Exit path: adding native response_format later is additive — an opt-in argument on @Agent that sets what **extra already forwards. The prompt path stays as the portable default, so nothing has to be removed.

docs.title: 0003 — An unpriced model reports zero cost, loudly
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-29 · Status: accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
estimate_cost() returns 0.0 for any model without an entry in the pricing table. The table shipped with OpenAI and Anthropic models only, while the README quickstart points users at Groq. Every run on the provider the docs recommend therefore reported total_cost: $0.000000 — indistinguishable from a genuinely free local model, and wrong in the one number the library claims as its differentiator.

Options: raise on an unknown model; guess a default price; or keep returning zero but stop being silent about it.

Raising is wrong — self-hosted models really are free, and a cost table has no business breaking a working pipeline. Guessing is worse than zero: a fabricated number is harder to notice than an obviously absent one.

The deeper problem is that any table baked into a release is stale on contact. Providers change prices; a bigger table postpones the failure without fixing its shape.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Unknown models keep costing 0.0, and the placeholder is made visible in two places:

  • warn_if_unpriced() logs once per process, from the LLM client where a model id first arrives, naming the model and the register_price() call that fixes it.
  • PipelineResult.unpriced_models lists every model in the run whose cost is a placeholder. A non-empty list means total_cost is an undercount.

estimate_cost() itself stays a pure function; the logging lives in a separate function called from the effectful edge.

The table is expanded to cover the providers the docs recommend, carries a review date, and documents register_price() as the authoritative override rather than the fallback.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Easier: a user on an unpriced model finds out from a log line and a result field instead of believing a wrong number. Pipelines never break because of a pricing gap. A test asserts the models named in the docs are priced, so the quickstart cannot silently regress to $0.

Harder: total_cost is still an undercount when a model is unpriced — unpriced_models tells you, but you have to look. The bundled prices remain indicative and will drift; they are documented as such rather than guaranteed.

Exit path: if the drift becomes a real support burden, the table moves to a data file refreshed independently of releases. The is_priced / warn_if_unpriced / unpriced_models surface is unaffected by where the numbers come from.

docs.title: 0004 - Side-effecting tools run at most once per run, through an effect ledger
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-11 · Status: accepted with amendments (2026-11-12)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Pipeline(retry_failed_agents=N) retries a failed agent by calling agent.execute() again from the top. Every tool call the first attempt made is made again. For a read tool that costs tokens. For a write tool it repeats the effect.

Reproduced on 0.7.1: an agent calls charge_card(customer="ali", amount=50), the next LLM call fails twice, the pipeline retries the agent, and the card is charged twice. output: done | charges executed: 2.

The in-loop duplicate guard in AgentSpec._run_tool_loop does not help: it only sees calls inside one attempt.

The research says this class of bug is general. "When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail" (arXiv 2609.15397) catalogs eight external-effect anomalies (missing, duplicated, surviving-aborted effects, ...) and finds that none of the capabilities needed to exclude them is fully expressible in MCP tool annotations across 98,291 registered tools. RetryBench (arXiv 2610.15884) shows models misuse idempotency keys depending on how a key is described. Leaving the decision to the model is not safe.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A tool opts in with @tool(side_effect=True). Default False: read tools behave exactly as today, with no ledger traffic.
  2. Pipeline(effect_ledger=...) turns protection on. No ledger, no change.
  3. Each side-effecting call gets a key: sha256(json([run_id, agent_name, tool_name, validated_args], sort_keys)). Validated args, so {"amount": "50"} and {"amount": 50} collide when the schema coerces them.
  4. Before running, the call claims the key. The ledger answers atomically:
  5. no record: caller owns it, record is PENDING, the tool runs;
  6. DONE: the stored result is returned, the tool does not run;
  7. FAILED: reclaimed, the tool runs again (the tool itself reported failure);
  8. PENDING: someone started this effect and never finished. The library cannot know whether it happened, so it raises EffectUncertainError, which the pipeline does not retry. A human decides.
  9. After running: success settles DONE with the stringified result; a raised exception settles FAILED; cancellation (timeout, crash) leaves PENDING.
  10. Ledger errors fail closed: if claim raises, the tool does not run.
  11. run_id widens from 8 to 32 hex characters. With a durable ledger, an 8-char id collides at roughly 65k runs (birthday bound) and a collision would replay another run's result.

Backends: InMemoryLedger (one process, covers in-run retries) and SqliteLedger (stdlib sqlite3, survives restarts and covers resume()). No new runtime dependency.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Retries and resume() stop repeating writes when a ledger is configured.
  • A crash between "effect happened" and "settled" surfaces as EffectUncertainError instead of a silent duplicate. That is the honest answer: only the tool's owner can check the outside world.
  • Two different agents making the same call in one run are two effects (the agent name is in the key). Intended.
  • The same call in two runs is two effects (the run id is in the key). Intended: serve() triggers are separate runs.
  • Compensation (undoing an effect after a later failure) is out of scope. It needs per-tool undo semantics and is a separate decision.
  • Swarm and swarm_routing call Tool.acall directly and are not covered.

docs.title: Amendments (2026-11-12)
docs.text:
Adopted for 0.8.0 with three changes, from the experiments that ran alongside it (agentflow-lab, EXP-B B1 on real ROS 2 with a real model):

  1. The key includes the occurrence number. With (run_id, agent, tool, args) alone, the second identical command in a run replays the first one's result and does not act: a real model sent the same move twice in 3 of 10 runs, and both were meant. The key is sha256([run_id, agent, canonical(tool, validated_args), n]), where n counts earlier calls with the same tool and validated arguments in the agent's current conversation. A retry starts a new conversation, so its first call is n=0 again and replays; a resume continues the saved conversation, so the count continues (it is rebuilt from the trace). Write calls run one at a time, so the count follows the model's order.
  2. The flag is effect="write" from ADR 0006, not side_effect=True.
  3. The ledger is always on for write tools. Without effect_ledger=, each run gets its own InMemoryLedger, which covers retries in one process and is freed with the run. A durable ledger is needed for resume() in a new process; a pipeline with a memory backend and write tools but no durable ledger warns once.

EffectUncertainError is exported from agentflow (it is raised out of Pipeline.run). The ledger classes stay in the opt-in module agentflow.effects. Using the same claim for HITL resume() (HITL-2, HITL-3) is the next step of 0.8.0.

docs.title: 0005 - The budget is enforced by reservation, and must be measurable
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-11 · Status: accepted · Narrows: 0003

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
budget_usd was documented as a hard ceiling, but it was checked once after each DAG level, from the costs on the surviving agent results. Measured on 0.7.1:

  • A level of 10 parallel agents on a $0.10 budget spent $1.00 before the check ran (COST-2).
  • A ReAct loop is one agent, so the check never ran inside it: 41 calls and $4.10 on a $0.10 budget (COST-3).
  • An agent attempt that failed and was retried billed real money that no result carried, so neither the total nor the check saw it (COST-1).
  • A model with no price costs 0.0 by ADR 0003, so the budget silently never fired: 10M tokens on a $0.000001 budget, status=completed (COST-4).

A ceiling that is checked after the money is spent, against numbers that omit some of the money, is not a ceiling.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Reserve before every call. LLM.generate reserves the worst case before it sends a request: the estimated prompt (3 characters per token, deliberately pessimistic) plus max_tokens of completion, at the model's price. After the call it settles to the billed amount. A cache hit reserves nothing.
  2. Wait, then refuse. A reservation that does not fit waits while other calls are in flight, because they usually settle below their reservation. When nothing is in flight and it still does not fit, the call raises BudgetExceededError.
  3. The refusal is sticky for the run. Every later call in the run raises the same error, so an agent that catches or wraps it (a supervisor turning a worker failure into an observation, the tool loop wrapping it in AgentError) cannot keep spending. The pipeline re-raises the original error and does not retry the agent: retrying cannot make a full budget fit.
  4. One measurement per run. The run scope (_scope.py) counts every billed call, including attempts whose result was discarded, across a HITL pause and resume(). BudgetExceededError.spent_usd and partial_result.total_cost use it.
  5. A budget must be measurable. With budget_usd set, a model without a registered price raises PipelineError before any request, naming the model and the fix. A local or free model is declared with register_price(model, prompt_per_1m=0, completion_per_1m=0). Without a budget, ADR 0003 holds unchanged: unpriced models cost 0.0, loudly.
  6. The check after each level stays as a backstop for agents that report cost without going through LLM.generate.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The ceiling holds against parallel siblings and inside tool loops. The overshoot is bounded by how far a reply exceeds its own reservation, which only happens if the 3-characters-per- token estimate is wrong for a prompt.
  • Runs near their budget stop earlier than before, by up to one reservation.
  • A large max_tokens makes reservations large. A run whose budget is smaller than one reservation stops before its first call. That is correct, and the error says how much was spent (nothing).
  • Every Ollama user who sets a budget needs one register_price line. The quickstart shows it.
  • An LLM subclass that overrides generate bypasses both reservation and measurement. The replacement seam for tests and custom providers is _complete (0.8.0, step 6).
  • The provider may bill a more specific model id than the one requested. Reservation uses the requested id; billing uses the reported one. If only the requested id is priced, the call is measured at 0.0. Not observed with the built-in price table, which matches by prefix.

docs.title: 0006 - Tools declare their effect: read, write, or unset
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-12 · Status: accepted · Related: 0004

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The tool loop treated every tool the same way, and each choice was wrong for some tool:

  • A duplicate-call guard rejected a repeated call with the same arguments. For a sensor read that is a normal request (LOOP-1: 33 rejections in 5 real robot runs). For a motion command it is a refused order (NEW-14: "forward 1 m, again" rejected 5 times in 10 runs).
  • Calls in one model reply ran concurrently. For two motion commands on one topic that interleaved contradictory commands (NEW-12, 5/5 runs on real ROS 2).
  • retry_failed_agents re-ran the whole agent, so a write repeated (ADR 0004).

The library cannot infer what a tool does. Two booleans (read_only, side_effect) allow a contradictory pair. One field with three states says it once.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
effect: Literal["read", "write"] | None = None on tool() and Tool.

Behaviour "read" "write" unset (None) Runs concurrently with other calls in a reply yes no: one at a time, in the model's order yes (unchanged) Duplicate-call guard off off on (unchanged) Effect ledger (ADR 0004) no yes, keyed by occurrence no Agent may be retried after running it yes yes, the ledger replays it no Sync function allowed yes no, TypeError at decoration yes

Why unset stays concurrent and guarded: existing pipelines keep their speed and behaviour.

Why unset blocks retries: a silent duplicate (an email sent twice, a card charged twice, a robot moved twice) is the worst outcome the library can produce, and it cannot tell whether an unset tool is that kind. The error names the tools and says to set effect. This is a behaviour change for retry_failed_agents users whose agents use unset tools.

Why write tools must be async: a sync function runs in a thread that cannot be cancelled, so it keeps acting after a timeout (NEW-07: 2.5 s of motion after the timeout on real ROS 2).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Robot and side-effect tools get the right semantics by declaring one word.
  • Tools without a declaration behave as in 0.7, except that their agents are not retried.
  • Write calls in one reply are slower than before, because they no longer overlap. Reads are unaffected.
  • Swarm and SupervisorAgent workers call Tool.acall directly, outside the tool loop, so serialization and the ledger do not cover them yet.

docs.title: Cost tracking
docs.text:
Every result carries an estimated USD cost, computed from built-in per-model pricing and the actual prompt/completion token split.

result = await pipe.run("Summarize the news")

agent = result.get("summarizer")
print(f"Agent cost:    ${agent.cost:.6f}")
print(f"Pipeline cost: ${result.total_cost:.6f}")

Cache hits bill nothing, so their cost is 0.0 while token counts remain for reference.

Prices use longest-prefix matching, so gpt-4o-2024-08-06 resolves to gpt-4o.

docs.title: Models with no price
docs.text:
A model that is not in the pricing table costs 0.0. For a local Ollama or vLLM model that is the truth; for a hosted model it is a placeholder, and total_cost is an undercount. agentflow never lets that pass silently — the model is logged once per process, and the run reports it:

if result.unpriced_models:
    print(f"no price for: {result.unpriced_models}")

docs.title: Custom or self-hosted models
docs.text:
register_price() is the authoritative override. The bundled table is indicative and drifts as providers change their prices, so anything you bill against should be registered explicitly:

from agentflow import register_price

register_price("my-finetuned-model", prompt_per_1m=0.50, completion_per_1m=1.50)

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
budget_usd is a hard ceiling on a single run. Every LLM call reserves its worst-case cost (estimated prompt plus max_tokens) before it is sent and settles to the billed amount after, so parallel agents and tool loops cannot run past it. The error carries the work that already completed, so tripping the ceiling does not throw away what you paid for:

from agentflow import BudgetExceededError

pipe = Pipeline(llm=llm, budget_usd=0.25)
try:
    result = await pipe.run("Analyze the filing")
except BudgetExceededError as exc:
    print(f"stopped at ${exc.spent_usd:.4f} of ${exc.budget_usd:.2f}")
    result = exc.partial_result

for name, agent_result in result.results.items():
    print(name, agent_result.cost)

A reservation that does not fit waits for in-flight calls to settle, then the run stops. The stop is final for the run: agents that catch the error cannot keep spending, and the pipeline does not retry them. The total includes attempts whose result was discarded, such as a failed attempt that was retried.

A budget needs a price for the model. A model without one raises PipelineError before the first call. For a local model, declare it free: register_price("llama3.2", prompt_per_1m=0, completion_per_1m=0). See ADR 0005.

docs.title: Token streaming
docs.text:
For interactive UIs, stream the model's output token-by-token with LLM.astream():

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are concise."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain async pipelines in one line."},
]
async for token in llm.astream(messages):
    print(token, end="", flush=True)

astream() honours the rate limiter but does not cache or retry (both are ambiguous mid-stream); use generate() for those.

See the full API in the reference.

docs.title: Memory & Context
docs.text: Agents in agentflow can share state across pipeline executions through a pluggable memory layer. This lets you build persistent, cross-session workflows where agents recall prior outputs without passing context manually.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every agent that has a memory backend attached will, on each execution:

  1. Load all prior outputs for its session from the store.
  2. Inject them into the system prompt as a [Memory] block (each entry is truncated to 300 characters).
  3. Save its own output back to the store after completion.

The Pipeline propagates a session_id to every agent before execution, so all agents in the same run automatically target the same session namespace.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Pass an InMemoryContext instance to the pipeline (or individual agents) and set a session_id:

from agentflow import LLM, Agent, Pipeline, InMemoryContext

# Create a shared memory store
memory = InMemoryContext(default_ttl=3600, max_entries=500)

llm = LLM(model="gpt-4o-mini", api_key="...")

@Agent(name="researcher", role="Research Analyst")
async def researcher(task: str, context: dict) -> str:
    return f"Research: {task}"

@Agent(name="writer", role="Content Writer")
async def writer(task: str, context: dict) -> str:
    return f"Write about: {task}"

# Phase 1: Researcher saves findings to memory
pipe1 = Pipeline(llm=llm, memory=memory, session_id="blog-42")
pipe1.add(researcher)
await pipe1.run("Edge AI in 2025")

# Phase 2: Writer recalls Researcher's findings from memory
pipe2 = Pipeline(llm=llm, memory=memory, session_id="blog-42")
pipe2.add(writer)
await pipe2.run("Edge AI in 2025")

The Writer's system prompt will automatically include the Researcher's output from Phase 1, even though the two agents run in separate pipelines.

Session ID is the bridge

Pipelines that share a session_id and a BaseMemory backend will see each other's stored context. Different session IDs are fully isolated — use them to partition knowledge.

docs.title: InMemoryContext
docs.text:
InMemoryContext is a lightweight, in-process implementation backed by a Python dictionary. It requires no external dependencies and is ideal for development, testing, and single-process deployments.

from agentflow import InMemoryContext

memory = InMemoryContext(
    default_ttl=3600,     # entries expire after 1 hour (default)
    max_entries=1000,      # LRU eviction per session (default; 0 = unlimited)
)

docs.title: TTL (Time-To-Live)
docs.text:
Every stored entry carries an expiration timestamp. When entries are loaded via load_context(), stale entries are purged automatically. This prevents memory bloat in long-running processes.

# Entries live for 5 minutes
memory = InMemoryContext(default_ttl=300)

Monotonic clock

TTL is measured against time.monotonic(), so system clock changes won't cause premature expiry.

docs.title: LRU Eviction
docs.text:
When a session exceeds max_entries, the least-recently-used entry is evicted to make room. This keeps memory bounded without manual cleanup.

# Allow at most 50 entries per session
memory = InMemoryContext(max_entries=50)

# When the 51st entry is saved under a session, the oldest entry is dropped.

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text: All InMemoryContext operations are guarded by an asyncio.Lock, making them safe for concurrent use within a single event loop. For multi-process or distributed setups, use RedisContext instead.

docs.title: RedisContext
docs.text:
Backed by Redis, suitable for multi-process and distributed deployments where memory must survive process restarts.

from agentflow import RedisContext

memory = RedisContext(
    url="redis://localhost:6379/0",
    prefix="agentflow:mem:",  # key namespace
    ttl=86400,                 # optional: expire entire session hash after 24h
)

Data is stored as a Redis hash per session, with all values JSON-serialised. An optional global ttl parameter expires the entire hash after every write.

Requires redis package

Install the extra: pip install agentflowkit[redis]

docs.title: VectorContext
docs.text:
Powered by ChromaDB, this backend stores context as vector embeddings, enabling semantic search over historical agent outputs.

from agentflow import VectorContext

# In-memory ChromaDB (ephemeral)
memory = VectorContext(collection_name="agent_history")

# Persistent storage on disk
memory = VectorContext(
    collection_name="agent_history",
    persist_dir="./chroma_data",
)

# With a custom embedding function
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

ef = embedding_functions.OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(api_key="...")
memory = VectorContext(embedding_fn=ef)

Call search_context() to find semantically relevant past outputs:

results = await memory.search_context("edge computing latency", top_k=3)
for r in results:
    print(r["document"], r["distance"])

Requires chromadb package

Install the extra: pip install agentflowkit[redis]

docs.title: BaseMemory interface
docs.text:
All memory backends implement the same abstract interface. You can swap implementations without changing agent code:

from agentflow import BaseMemory

class BaseMemory(ABC):
    async def save_context(self, session_id: str, key: str, value: Any) -> None: ...
    async def load_context(self, session_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
    async def clear(self, session_id: str) -> None: ...
    async def delete_key(self, session_id: str, key: str) -> None: ...

To implement a custom backend (e.g., Postgres, S3), subclass BaseMemory and implement these four methods. Pass your instance to the pipeline and it will be used automatically.

docs.title: Example: multi-agent shared memory
docs.text:
The file examples/memory_chat_agents.py demonstrates a complete workflow where a Researcher and Writer share context across two pipeline runs:

python examples/memory_chat_agents.py

See the full API in the reference.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Pipeline.run() is silent by default. Pass a Hooks instance to observe the full lifecycle and bridge it to logging, metrics, OpenTelemetry, or Langfuse. All hook methods are no-ops by default, so override only what you need — and a hook that raises is caught and warned rather than crashing the pipeline.

docs.title: Structured logging out of the box
docs.text:
LoggingHooks emits structured JSON logs via PipelineLogger:

from agentflow import Pipeline, LoggingHooks

pipe = Pipeline(llm=llm, hooks=LoggingHooks("research-pipeline"))
result = await pipe.run("AI in Healthcare")
# {"timestamp": "...", "event": "agent_complete", "agent": "writer", "tokens": 812, ...}

docs.title: Custom hooks
docs.text:
Subclass Hooks to send spans to your own backend:

from agentflow import Hooks

class OTelHooks(Hooks):
    def on_agent_start(self, agent: str, level: int) -> None:
        self._spans[agent] = tracer.start_span(agent)

    def on_agent_end(self, result) -> None:
        span = self._spans.pop(result.agent)
        span.set_attribute("tokens", result.tokens_used)
        span.set_attribute("cost_usd", result.cost)
        span.end()

pipe = Pipeline(llm=llm, hooks=OTelHooks())

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
Every run that starts ends with exactly one of on_pipeline_end or on_pipeline_error (a run that pauses for approval ends with neither). on_pipeline_error(error, run_id) also fires for a budget stop and for a cancellation, so a trace span never stays open. stream() fires the same pipeline hooks as run().

A tool that fails, is refused for invalid arguments, or is asked for under a name the agent does not have calls on_tool_error(agent, tool, error), and is listed on the result:

result = await pipe.run(task)
for failure in result.tool_errors:
    # {"agent": "pilot", "tool": "move", "effect": "write", "kind": "failed", "error": "..."}
    print(failure)

kind is "failed", "invalid_arguments" or "unknown_tool". result.status stays "completed" because the model usually recovers, so this list is how you learn that a write tool may have left the world in an unknown state.

docs.title: Streaming events
docs.text:
For live progress in the same process, use pipeline.stream() instead — it yields Event objects (agent_start, agent_complete, agent_skipped, pipeline_complete, …) as they happen:

async for event in pipe.stream("AI in Healthcare"):
    if event.type == "agent_complete":
        print(event.agent, event.data["tokens"], event.data["cached"])

See the full API in the reference.

docs.title: Tools & Function Calling
docs.text: Tools turn an agent from a one-shot prompt into a real ReAct agent: the model decides which functions to call, agentflow executes them, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model produces a final answer.

docs.title: Define a tool
docs.text:
Decorate any Python function with @tool. The JSON schema is generated automatically from the type hints — you never hand-write it. Sync and async functions both work (sync tools run in a thread so they never block the loop).

from agentflow import tool

@tool
def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> str:
    """Look up the current weather for a city."""  # (1)!
    return f"18°{unit[0].upper()} and sunny in {city}"
  1. The docstring becomes the tool description the model sees. city is required (no default); unit is optional.

docs.title: Attach tools to an agent
docs.text:
from agentflow import Agent, Pipeline, LLM

@Agent(name="assistant", role="Helpful Assistant", tools=[get_weather])
async def assistant(task: str, context: dict) -> str:
    return task

pipe = Pipeline(llm=LLM(model="gpt-4o-mini", api_key="..."))
pipe.add(assistant)
result = await pipe.run("What's the weather in Amman in fahrenheit?")

The loop is bounded by max_tool_iterations (default 6) so a misbehaving model can never spin forever.

docs.title: Inspect what happened
docs.text:
Every tool call is recorded in the agent result's metadata:

for call in result.get("assistant").metadata["tool_calls"]:
    print(call["tool"], call["arguments"], "->", call["result"])

docs.title: Declare what a tool does
docs.text:
Say whether a tool only observes or changes the world:

@tool(effect="read")
async def get_pose() -> str: ...          # may be repeated, retried, run in parallel

@tool(effect="write")
async def move(linear: float, duration_s: float) -> str: ...   # recorded, never repeated

A write tool runs one call at a time in the order the model asked, and each call runs at most once per run: if the pipeline retries the agent, a call that already completed returns its stored result instead of acting again. Sending the same command twice is two calls and both run. A write tool must be async.

A tool without effect behaves as in 0.7, with one difference: an agent that ran it is not retried by retry_failed_agents, because the retry could repeat it.

If an earlier attempt started a write and never finished, the library cannot know whether it happened. It raises EffectUncertainError instead of guessing. To make this survive a restart, give the pipeline a durable ledger:

from agentflow.effects import SqliteLedger

pipe = Pipeline(llm=llm, retry_failed_agents=2, effect_ledger=SqliteLedger("effects.db"))

See ADR 0004 and ADR 0006.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
If a tool's arguments fail validation or the function raises, the error is fed back to the model as the tool result (prefixed Error:) so it can recover, rather than crashing the pipeline. Validation is strict: an argument the tool does not declare, or NaN or Infinity in a number, is refused rather than dropped or passed on.

Tool output longer than tool_output_max_chars (default 5000) is truncated with a marker. When the agent reaches max_tool_iterations, it gets one last call without tools to answer from what it found. A ToolError is raised only when you call a tool directly via Tool.acall.

See the full API in the reference.
